claim: Tangerine Computer Systems designed the Oric-1, and Oric Products International launched it with financial backing from British Car Auctions.
evidence: Computer & Video Games issue 13, November 1982, p. 89
Personal Computer Games issue 1, Summer 1983, pp. 33-35
Your Computer, February 1983, pp. 46-49 (Meirion Jones, Oric review)
Your Computer, February 1988, pp. 67-69 ('Ghosts in the machine')
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: PCG p. 33 calls Oric 'the new company'. Retro Gamer says 'Tangerine became Oric Products International'. YC Feb 1983 p. 49 also names British Car Auctions as a backer.

claim: Dr Paul Johnson and Barry Muncaster founded Tangerine in October 1979; its earlier products included the 6502-based Microtan 65 kit.
evidence: Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: The prose attributes it to Retro Gamer. Your Computer, January 1985, p. 69 confirms only that 'Paul and Barry' were 'heavily involved in Tangerine' and now ran Oric.

claim: The Oric 1 was announced in late 1982 as a Spectrum rival, with the 16K model planned for £99 and due that October.
evidence: Computer & Video Games issue 13, November 1982, p. 89
Your Computer, July 1985, p. 13 ('Eureka for Oric: Normans conquer Atmos')

claim: Oric launched the machine in January 1983, but delivery was slow and the first machines carried EPROMs instead of the final ROM.
evidence: Sinclair User issue 13, April 1983, p. 16
Your Computer, January 1983, pp. 28, 60
Personal Computer Games issue 1, Summer 1983, pp. 33-35
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: Quotes checked against the scans: the Tullis quote and 'streaming off the production line' (YC p. 28), 'comical inability', 'extremely good value' and 'two EPROMs' (PCG), and the SU line on peripheral prototypes with no definite dates.

claim: Advance-order figures differ: in January 1983 Your Computer reported 250,000 orders already placed, while Retro Gamer later gave over 30,000 pre-orders.
evidence: Your Computer, January 1983, pp. 28, 60
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: These figures disagree. The entry presents both as reported figures.

claim: The 48K model sold at £169.95 (about £170). The 16K model was expected in shops by early July 1983 at £129.95, a summer-sale deal with software, against the £99 first planned.
evidence: Personal Computer Games issue 1, Summer 1983, pp. 33-35
Personal Computer News issue 14, 10-15 June 1983, p. 6 ('More micro cuts')
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: PCN 14 is printed p. 6 and dated 10-15 June 1983. YC Jan 1983 gave a planned 48K price of £175. Retro Gamer says the 16K appeared in May. PCG calls £170 'slightly dearer than the 48k Spectrum', while Retro Gamer says it was a fiver cheaper. The entry attributes the comparison to PCG.

claim: The Oric-1 had 57 individually moving plastic keys, between a full keyboard and the Spectrum's rubber keys, and came with a Centronics printer port and an RGB socket as standard.
evidence: Personal Computer Games issue 1, Summer 1983, pp. 33-35
Bits & Bytes (New Zealand) vol. 2 no. 4, December 1983/January 1984, pp. 29-30 (Nick Alexander, 'Oric 1: Impressive small machine')
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47

claim: The machine used a 6502-family processor (a 6502A at 1MHz in the Atmos) with 16K of ROM holding an extended Microsoft BASIC.
evidence: Your Computer, March 1984, pp. 64-65 (David Scobie, Atmos review)
Bits & Bytes (New Zealand) vol. 2 no. 4, December 1983/January 1984, pp. 29-30 (Nick Alexander, 'Oric 1: Impressive small machine')
Personal Computer Games issue 1, Summer 1983, pp. 33-35
qualification: Only Your Computer gives the 1MHz clock.

claim: Sound came from a General Instrument AY-3-8912 three-channel sound generator. A 6522 VIA, working with the AY's I/O port to scan the keyboard, handled keyboard, tape and printer I/O.
evidence: Service Manual for the Oric-1 and Oric Atmos Microcomputers (Oric Products International, 1984), pp. 10-11, 16-20, 46, 53, 69-72
Oric-1 48K circuit diagram BN0130 (Oric Products International), issue 7, 24-2-84
qualification: The part number rests on the manufacturer's own documents, which share a provenance. Bits & Bytes and YC Feb 1983 confirm a three-channel sound chip without naming it. Retro Gamer 29 p. 44 says AY-3-8910; the entry follows the parts list and records the disagreement. 'The Spectrum had only a beeper' is supported by Retro Gamer 29 p. 44. The account of the AY playing on its own after register writes agrees with the reviewed hardware/ay-3-8912 entry.

claim: The display used serial attributes: invisible control characters that set colour, flashing or double height for the rest of a line. It offered eight colours, a 40 x 28 text screen and a 240 x 200 HIRES screen.
evidence: Bob Maunder, The Oric-1 Companion (LINSAC, Middlesbrough, first printing September 1983), pp. 86-88
Your Computer, March 1984, pp. 64-65 (David Scobie, Atmos review)
Your Computer, February 1983, pp. 46-49 (Meirion Jones, Oric review)
Bits & Bytes (New Zealand) vol. 2 no. 4, December 1983/January 1984, pp. 29-30 (Nick Alexander, 'Oric 1: Impressive small machine')
Peter Lupton and Frazer Robinson, The Oric Atmos Handbook (Century Communications, London, 1984)
Personal Computer Games issue 1, Summer 1983, pp. 33-35
qualification: Maunder's quote and the 240 x 200 grid, 40 locations a line and six-pixel patterns checked against the text, with the title page (LINSAC, first printing September 1983).

claim: Programs saved to tape at 2,400 baud, with a slower 300 baud option.
evidence: Your Computer, February 1983, pp. 46-49 (Meirion Jones, Oric review)
Bits & Bytes (New Zealand) vol. 2 no. 4, December 1983/January 1984, pp. 29-30 (Nick Alexander, 'Oric 1: Impressive small machine')
qualification: 'for extra security' is a verbatim YC quote.

claim: Oric promised a Prestel modem and a teletext-compatible character set from the start; a Prestel adaptor was still being announced in mid-1984.
evidence: Your Computer, January 1983, pp. 28, 60
Your Computer, February 1983, pp. 46-49 (Meirion Jones, Oric review)
Personal Computer News, 2 June 1984, pp. 2-3, 18

claim: Oric cut its prices after Sinclair cut the Spectrum's in May 1983; by early 1984 W H Smith listed the 48K Oric-1 at £139.95.
evidence: Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
W H Smith advertisement, Your Computer, February 1984, p. 8
qualification: The price-cut sequence rests on Retro Gamer alone and is attributed in the prose. The W H Smith price was checked on the YC Feb 1984 p. 8 scan and is cited in the entry's Sources.

claim: A fire at the Feltham factory in October 1983 wiped out much of Oric's Christmas production.
evidence: Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: Attributed to Retro Gamer in the prose. A later Retro Gamer issue repeats it; that is not independent.

claim: About 160,000 Oric-1s were sold during 1983.
evidence: Big K issue 1, April 1984, p. 8
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: Presented as a reported figure. Big K's 'over 160K' probably repeats Oric's own claim, and Retro Gamer calls it an estimate for UK sales. YC Jan 1985 quotes Muncaster claiming 350,000 sold in two years; the entry does not use that figure.

claim: Edenspring Investments rescued Oric financially in October 1983, but the sources disagree on the amount.
evidence: Personal Computer News issue 97, 2 February 1985, p. 2
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
Your Computer, February 1988, pp. 67-69 ('Ghosts in the machine')
Sinclair User issue 37, April 1985, p. 7
qualification: PCN 97 (printed p. 2, dated 2 February 1985) reports 25 million new Edenspring shares raising £750,000, with debts of £1.01 million at the time. Retro Gamer gives £4 million. The entry gives both.

claim: The Oric Atmos replaced the Oric-1 at the Which Computer? Show in January 1984. It used the same circuit board, still marked 'Oric-1', with a black and red case, typewriter-style keys and a revised ROM that fixed bugs and added tape verify, join and array STORE/RECALL.
evidence: Your Computer, March 1984, pp. 64-65 (David Scobie, Atmos review)
Personal Computer News, 8 December 1984, p. 2 (as paginated)
Big K issue 1, April 1984, p. 8
Service Manual for the Oric-1 and Oric Atmos Microcomputers (Oric Products International, 1984), pp. 10-11, 16-20, 46, 53, 69-72
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: PCN names the show and dates the Stratos's French debut 'close to the first anniversary of the Atmos'. Retro Gamer gives the Oric-1's discontinuation as January 1984. No source states 'January' alongside the show name; the month is an inference from the two.

claim: The Atmos cost about £170 in Britain and 2,400FF in France in mid-1984.
evidence: Personal Computer News, 2 June 1984, pp. 2-3, 18
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: Only PCN gives the French price.

claim: The Microdisc, a 3-inch disk drive with a CP/M-like DOS, finally arrived in 1984 at £270 including VAT, more than a year after it was first promised.
evidence: Personal Computer News, 2 June 1984, pp. 2-3, 18
Pixel (Greece) issue 4, September 1984, p. 59
qualification: PCN's OCR reads '3.25 inch' Hitachi drives. Pixel gives 3-inch Hitachi FC-1 disks. Check the PCN scan.

claim: The Oric did better in France than in Britain. Loriciels published Oric and Atmos games there, and a French syndicate including Oric's French distributor ASN bid for the company.
evidence: Personal Computer News, 2 June 1984, pp. 2-3, 18
Personal Computer News issue 99, 16 February 1985, p. 2
Your Computer, February 1988, pp. 67-69 ('Ghosts in the machine')
Your Computer, July 1985, p. 13 ('Eureka for Oric: Normans conquer Atmos')
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47

claim: Around 50,000 Oric-1s were sold in France in 1983, and the French magazine Théoric was devoted to the machine.
evidence: Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: From Retro Gamer's sidebar and attributed to it in the prose.

claim: The Oric was sold and covered beyond Britain and France: Barr Bros were sole agents in New Zealand, DATAKOR imported the Microdisc into Greece, Greece's Pixel printed Oric 1 listings from its first issue, and Yugoslavia's Svet kompjutera ran Oric material.
evidence: Bits & Bytes (New Zealand) vol. 2 no. 4, December 1983/January 1984, pp. 29-30 (Nick Alexander, 'Oric 1: Impressive small machine')
Pixel (Greece) issue 4, September 1984, p. 59
Svet kompjutera (Yugoslavia), June 1986, p. 51
qualification: Each market rests on one period source, stated separately. 'SOLE N.Z. AGENTS' confirmed on Bits & Bytes p. 30. The twelve-machine list comes from the reviewed magazines/pixel entry.

claim: Oric's next machine, the 64K Stratos (to be called IQ164 in Britain), was shown at the Frankfurt fair but never went on sale from Oric.
evidence: Personal Computer News, 8 December 1984, p. 2 (as paginated)
Personal Computer News issue 97, 2 February 1985, p. 2
Personal Computer News issue 99, 16 February 1985, p. 2
Your Computer, July 1985, p. 13 ('Eureka for Oric: Normans conquer Atmos')
Your Computer, February 1988, pp. 67-69 ('Ghosts in the machine')
qualification: The specs (64K RAM, 6502, two ROM slots) are PCN's own description. Everiss is quoted only on compatibility. PCN 97 and YC January 1985 also call Tansoft Oric's software arm.

claim: Oric called in the receiver in February 1985, with debts estimated at £5.5 million, 'especially to Edenspring Investments'.
evidence: Personal Computer News issue 99, 16 February 1985, p. 2
Sinclair User issue 37, April 1985, p. 7
Your Computer, July 1985, p. 13 ('Eureka for Oric: Normans conquer Atmos')
Your Computer, February 1988, pp. 67-69 ('Ghosts in the machine')
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: Corrected from 'mostly owed to Edenspring'; Sinclair User says 'especially'. Retro Gamer says more than £5 million.

claim: In 1985 the French distributor Eureka Informatique bought Oric's rights and stock and moved Atmos assembly to its plant in Normandy.
evidence: Your Computer, July 1985, p. 13 ('Eureka for Oric: Normans conquer Atmos')
Your Computer, February 1988, pp. 67-69 ('Ghosts in the machine')
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: YC 1988 dates the purchase to June 1985. The Normandy plant appears only in the July 1985 report, which says the move would happen 'later this month'.

claim: Under Eureka the new Oric was the Telestrat (1986), built for France's Minitel network.
evidence: Svet kompjutera (Yugoslavia), June 1986, p. 51
Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
qualification: Changed from 'the last Oric', which no source supports. The Minitel design, the September 1986 sale date, the £400 price and the 6,000 sales come from Retro Gamer alone and are attributed. Svet kompjutera reports the machine as coming soon ('Uskoro novi Oric telestrat').

claim: Oric software came from British houses including Tansoft, IJK, Ocean, Durell, Level 9 and Melbourne House (whose The Hobbit kept its pictures on the Oric), and from French publishers such as Loriciels, which published Éric Chahi's Doggy and Louis-Marie Rocques's L'Aigle d'Or.
evidence: Martyn Carroll, 'Retroinspection: Oric-1', Retro Gamer issue 29 (2006), pp. 42-47
Personal Computer News, 2 June 1984, pp. 2-3, 18
Personal Computer Games issue 3, February 1984
'In the chair with... Eric Chahi', Retro Gamer Collection vol. 7 (2013), pp. 186-191
qualification: These credits agree with the reviewed entries games/the-hobbit (PCG 3), companies/level-9, people/eric-chahi and companies/silmarils. For Ocean, Durell and IJK the only evidence is Retro Gamer 29 p. 45 ('pledged their support early on'); the reviewed companies/ocean-software and companies/durell entries do not mention Oric releases.
